issues.legal_issue: A later mineral lease does not include minerals expressly excluded by an earlier lease when the later document, read as a whole, preserves the earlier lease’s exclusions.
material_facts: An earlier lease granted mining rights over specified minerals but expressly excluded certain stones and other materials.
A later lease granted rights over minerals not covered by the earlier grant, referred to the earlier lease, and preserved its terms except where inconsistent with the later lease.
The later lease made subleases subject to the earlier lease’s exclusion clause and stated that the earlier lease remained valid and subsisting.
The dispute prompting the later lease concerned minerals not mentioned in the earlier granting clause, and there was no evidence of a prior dispute about the exclusion clause.
The alleged dispossession concerned only minerals excluded by the earlier lease.
issues.conclusion: The minerals excluded by the earlier lease were not included in the later lease, so the claimed dispossession of those minerals did not support suspension of rent.
issues.legal_principle: The parties’ intention in a grant is determined from their words, presumed to be used in their strict grammatical sense. If a clear earlier disposition is irreconcilable with a later provision, the earlier disposition prevails. If the document is ambiguous, the court reads it as a whole to ascertain intention and, if ambiguity remains, construes it strictly against the grantor and in favour of the grantee. The Court approved Annapagonda v. Sangadiappa, (1901) Bom. L.R. 221 (F.B.); Rashbehari v. Anand Ram, 43 Cal. 211; Ramcharan Das v. Gaya Prasad, 30 All. 422; Lakshumanan v. Sadayappa, A.I.R. 1919 Mad. 816; and Thankamma v. Kunhamma, A.I.R. 1919 Mad. 370. It considered Currimbhai v. Ahmedali, 58 Bom. 505, and Lakshmanan Chetty v. Sadayappa Chetty, 35 M.L.J. 571.

rule.if: later_lease_construction_case and earlier_lease_expressly_excluded_assets and later_lease_referred_to_earlier_lease and (later_subleases_were_subject_to_earlier_terms or later_lease_preserved_earlier_lease) and later_dispute_concerned_unmentioned_assets

predicates.later_lease_construction_case: The case concerns the construction of a later grant made in relation to an earlier grant.
predicates.earlier_lease_expressly_excluded_assets: The earlier grant expressly excluded specified assets from its grant.
predicates.later_lease_referred_to_earlier_lease: The later grant referred to the earlier grant and its terms.
predicates.later_subleases_were_subject_to_earlier_: The later grant made subgrants subject to terms of the earlier grant.
predicates.later_lease_preserved_earlier_lease: The later grant stated that the earlier grant remained valid or subsisting.
predicates.later_dispute_concerned_unmentioned_asse: The parties made the later grant to resolve a dispute about assets not mentioned in the earlier grant.

issues.definition: When a later-grant construction case has an earlier express exclusion and the later document’s terms and context preserve the earlier arrangement, the excluded assets remain outside the later grant.

issues.legal_issue: Clear acknowledgments of a debt by a prior receiver who incurred the liability can save a claim from limitation, even when payment is stated to follow acceptance of accompanying accounts.
material_facts: The claim sought recovery under a later lease granted to a receiver, and the present receiver derived the liability through a prior receiver.
Letters signed personally by prior receivers stated amounts of royalty as due to the lessor.
The letters separately stated that cheques would be sent after the accounts or amounts were accepted; that payment language did not make the statements of the debts conditional.
The suit was brought after the ordinary limitation period for part of the claim, and the acknowledgments relied on were made before that period expired.
issues.conclusion: The letters were acknowledgments within the meaning of section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and saved the claim from limitation for the earlier period.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1908, an acknowledgment of liability made in writing and signed before expiry of the limitation period saves limitation. A statement that an amount is due is not rendered conditional merely because a later sentence makes payment dependent on acceptance of accounts; the Court read the letters as independently acknowledging the debt. Because the earlier receivers had signed personally and the liability arose under a lease granted to a receiver, section 19 applied directly without recourse to Explanation II. The Court therefore did not decide whether a receiver is generally an agent of the estate owners for making acknowledgments.

rule.if: lease_debt_recovery_suit and liability_derived_through_prior_receiver and prior_receiver_signed_before_limitation_expired and signed_letter_independently_admitted_debt and payment_followed_account_acceptance

predicates.lease_debt_recovery_suit: The proceeding seeks recovery of a debt arising under a lease.
predicates.liability_derived_through_prior_receiver: The current representative’s liability derives through a prior receiver who incurred the debt.
predicates.prior_receiver_signed_before_limitation_: A prior receiver signed an acknowledgment before the applicable limitation period expired.
predicates.signed_letter_independently_admitted_deb: The signed letter stated that an amount was due independently of any later payment terms.
predicates.payment_followed_account_acceptance: The letter provided that payment would be made after the recipient accepted the accompanying account or amount.

issues.definition: In a lease-debt recovery suit, a prior receiver’s timely signed, independent admission of the debt saves the claim from limitation even if payment is to follow acceptance of accounts.

issues.legal_issue: An agent may be duly authorised to sign an acknowledgment either by the debtor’s act or by operation of law or court order.
material_facts: The limitation argument asserted that an agent’s authority to acknowledge a debt must come from the debtor.
The Court considered the statutory language, which did not restrict how the authority could be conferred, and approved earlier decisions recognizing authority conferred by law or court order.
The Court did not need to decide whether a receiver was, by that status alone, authorised to acknowledge the estate’s debts in this case.
issues.conclusion: The words ‘duly authorised’ include authority conferred by the debtor, by law, or by court order.
issues.legal_principle: Explanation II to section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1908, defines a signed acknowledgment to include one signed by an agent duly authorised in that behalf. The provision does not limit the source of authority to the debtor’s act. The Court approved Annapagonda v. Sangadiappa, (1901) Bom. L.R. 221 (F.B.); Rashbehari v. Anand Ram, 43 Cal. 211; Ramcharan Das v. Gaya Prasad, 30 All. 422; Lakshumanan v. Sadayappa, A.I.R. 1919 Mad. 816; and Thankamma v. Kunhamma, A.I.R. 1919 Mad. 370. It considered Currimbhai v. Ahmedali, 58 Bom. 505, and Lakshmanan Chetty v. Sadayappa Chetty, 35 M.L.J. 571.

predicates.agent_signed_debt_acknowledgment_case: The issue concerns whether an agent’s signature on a debt acknowledgment is authorised.
predicates.agent_authority_conferred_by_law_or_cour: The agent’s authority to sign the acknowledgment was conferred by law or by court order.

issues.definition: When an agent signs a debt acknowledgment and the agent’s authority comes from law or a court order, the signature is duly authorised.
